title.en: Kelauna and Ketsinsiltin: The Avenging Brothers

region.en: Okanagon country, Washington (symbolic pin at Okanogan River)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根故地，華盛頓州（象徵定位於奧卡諾根河）

texts.period: Told by Lalaha'p; collected by Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales (Gould), 1. Kelauna'

summary.en: When their father is killed by his enemies, the grown sons Grizzly-Bear (Kelauna) and Ketsinsiltin resolve on revenge; their uncle Mo'lski ferries them to the enemy camp, where they hide their poisoned arrows, then at midnight strike the killer in forehead, chest and back and escape. Attacked by the slain man's friends, Grizzly-Bear is struck in the forehead with a white arrow but is cared for by Grizzly-Bear his helper, while his brother fights on and kills all the enemies except one, sent back to tell the tale.
summary.zh: 父為敵所殺，二子長成，誓復父仇：格拉烏納（灰熊）與凱欽西爾廷。舅父莫爾斯基舟送二人至敵營，暗藏毒箭；夜半潛入仇人之帳，連中其額、胸、背而遁。仇家追擊，格拉烏納額中白箭，賴其守護靈『灰熊』救治；其弟奮戰，誅敵殆盡，唯留一人歸報。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: A man had been killed by his enemies. When his two sons were grown up, they decided to take revenge. Their names were Grizzly-Bear (Kelauna) and Ketsinsiltin. Their uncle, Mo'lski, took them in his canoe to the camp of their enemies. The young men hid their bows and poisoned arrows at the bank of the river. At midnight their uncle gave them their weapons, and they stole into the tent of the man who had killed their father; they hit him in the forehead, the chest, and the back, and made their escape.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 98 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the young men were attacked by the friends of the person whom they had killed, Grizzly-Bear was hit in the forehead with a white arrow. He was cared for by the Grizzly-Bear, his helper. His brother continued to fight, and killed all the enemies except one, who was sent back to tell the tale.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 98 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Left-Arm: The Wolf Brothers' Rescue

region.en: Okanagon country and the Columbia at Kettle Falls (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根故地與哥倫比亞河壺口瀑布（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Lalaha'p; collected by Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales (Gould), 2. Left-Arm'

summary.en: Left-Arm's sweat-bath steam betrays his home; enemies kill his parents and carry off his sister. Returning as three wolves with bows become wolf-tails, the brothers howl and are answered by their sister's song; they follow the war-party, scent it again with a grizzly-bear cape, steal the enemies' weapons at dawn and kill them with their own spears, sparing one man to tell the tale, while the oldest brother escapes across the river with the woman. Left-Arm later seeks his stolen love Ring-around-the-Ankle near Kettle Falls, is captured with her, and after five years of bondage they escape to the mountains; wounded in the hunt, he dies, and his wolf-dog — still carrying the rattlesnake-poison bone charm under its neck-skin — runs off to the wolves and will not come back.
summary.zh: 左臂汗浴之蒸氣洩其行蹤，敵人殺其父母，擄其妹。兄弟三人化狼而返（弓箭化為狼尾），長嗥相呼，妹以歌應之。他們尾隨敵蹤，復以灰熊皮披嗅跡尋至敵營，黎明潛入，竊其兵器，以敵之矛誅敵，僅留一人歸報；長兄則携妹渡河而遁。後左臂尋失蹤之戀人『踝環女』至壺口瀑布，二人俱被擒，囚五年乃逃，匿於山中獵駝鹿。一日獵中負傷，自知將死，囑妻携狼犬歸返娘家——狼犬頸皮下仍藏響尾蛇毒之骨符——犬竟奔狼群去，喚之不回。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Left-Arm (Tcatcl'ko) was taking a sweat-bath, and a dense cloud of steam was escaping through the top of the lodge. A short distance away some enemies saw the cloud of steam, and surmised that Left-Arm was taking his bath. They stole up to his home and killed his parents; his sister was carried away captive. Left-Arm and his brothers, who had been out hunting, followed the enemies, and overtook the war-party while they were sitting around a camp-fire, the young woman in the centre of the circle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 98 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Left-Arm had changed himself and his brothers into three wolves, their bows and arrows having become wolf-tails. They howled, and their sister, who recognized their voices, replied by singing; this made her captors suspicious, and they moved on, all the time watching her closely. The wolves followed them northward until the enemies camped again and covered the girl with a buffalo robe. When the brothers lost the trail, they resumed human form; one put on his grizzly-bear cape and was enabled to scent the trail. The enemies were asleep, and had piled their weapons together; before dawn the brothers stole into the camp, selected weapons, threw the others into the river, and killed the enemies with their own spears. The oldest brother took the woman and escaped with her across the river; all but one man was killed, and he was spared to return and tell his tribe what had happened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 98-99 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Left-Arm jumped into the water to swim across and find his brother and sister, but his bear-skin robe caught on a snag and he was in danger of drowning; suddenly the thought came, 'Why am I so foolish? I can turn into a frog, and the water will not hurt me' — and he did so, remaining in the water calling for his brothers until they brought the canoe and took him in. Later on Left-Arm fell in love with a maiden named Ring-around-the-Ankle, who was carried away by enemies from the Columbia River country to a place near Kettle Falls; he wandered long seeking her, his luck turned because a bone charm covered with rattlesnake-poison was embedded under the neck-skin of his wolf-dog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 99 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Finally he found her — she had carved a rock near the falls so that it resembled a canoe — and tried to escape with her; they were overtaken and captured, bound and beaten, and kept prisoners for five years. Finally they escaped and lived on the mountains hunting moose and other game. One day Left-Arm was wounded while hunting, and knew he was going to die; he told his wife to take the wolf-dog and return to her people, and his spirit passed away. The dog ran away and joined the wolves, still carrying the bone charm, and Ring-around-the-Ankle could not persuade it to return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 99 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Warrior and his Faithless Wife

region.en: Okanagon country and the Sioux plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根故地與蘇人平原（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Lalaha'p; collected by Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales (Gould), 3. The Warrior and his Faithless Wife'

summary.en: A chief's daughter is captured by the Sioux and held three years until a dream sends her home with the chief's knife and dress and three horses. Her brother raises a war-party for revenge, but on the trail his braves desert him; he seizes the Sioux chief's son while his wife holds the man's feet — she looks at the handsome Sioux, turns traitor, catches her own husband's feet, and the Sioux cuts his throat and carries her off. The husband revives among Blackfoot prisoners of the Sioux, raises a great war-party, is captured and killed in battle — but his heart will not burn, the spirit of the buffalo resuscitates him, and he goes to the chief's tent, draws his dagger, pulls his wife's head back by the braids and cuts it off, then returns to his own people.
summary.zh: 酋長之女為蘇人所擄，三年後夢示攜刀、衣、三馬而逃。其兄率眾復仇，然途中部眾四散；他獨自擒蘇酋之子，命其妻按住敵人雙足——妻見蘇人俊美，竟叛夫而握其足，蘇人割其喉，擄妻而去。武士重生，投奔為蘇人所囚之黑腳族，受善待；後率大軍再戰，兵敗被誅，焚其屍而心不化，野牛之靈救之復活。他直入酋帳，拔刀揪其妻辮而斬之，隨即歸返本族。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Historical war-tale framing; published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: In early days there were plenty of buffalo. Once a year the Okanagon, Sanpoil, Spokane, Moses, and Colville tribes joined, and crossed the mountains to hunt. One white moon (January) the Sioux pursued and captured a chief's daughter, and kept her captive for three years. One night the young woman dreamed that a spirit told her to take the chief's sharp knife, and the buckskin dress of the chief's wife; she obeyed and fled, taking also three horses. The next morning the fleetest braves were called on to pursue her, but she took off her robe, tied it into a bundle on her back, swam a river ahead of them, and reached her home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 99-100 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her brother wanted to revenge her capture, and took his band of braves and his wife, and started; on the way his braves deserted him, but still he went on. They saw the Sioux chief's son, and the Okanagon warrior said to his wife, 'When I try to capture him, take hold of his feet.' His wife looked at the Sioux and saw that he was very handsome; she turned traitor and caught her husband's feet. Then the Sioux cut his throat and left him, and carried the woman off as his slave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 100 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The husband recovered, and lingered in the neighborhood, killing all the Sioux who came in his way; he was discovered by a Blackfoot tribe who had been held prisoners by the Sioux, and they treated him kindly. After a while he returned home and raised a large war-party, joined by Blackfoot warriors; there was a pitched battle, in which he was captured and killed. The Sioux burned his body, but his heart could not be burnt; some friendly Indians wrapped his heart in a buffalo-skin, and the spirit of the buffalo resuscitated him. Then he went to the chief's tent, saw his wife sitting at the feet of the chief, drew his dagger, pulled her head back by her braids, and cut it off; then he went away to his own people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 100 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote Becomes Chief of the Salmon

region.en: Columbia and Okanagon rivers, Sanpoil country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞河與奧卡諾根河，桑普瓦故地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 1. Coyote becomes Chief of the Salmon'

summary.en: Coyote kills proud Sparrow for his beaded war head-dress, blind the Willow-Grouse children with pitch when he cannot understand their language, and is scared over a cliff by the revenging parents — turning into a basket that floats to the rock dam of two jealous sisters who keep all the silver-salmon. Taken in as a dish, then thrown into the fire, he emerges a little boy, grows digging at the dam with a horn on his head until the water bursts through — 'Women were never intended to guard salmon' — turns the sisters into water-snipe and kildee, and leads the salmon upstream. When the echoing-voiced girl he loves refuses him, he dams the Similkameen, Okanagon, Kettle and Columbia with falls to keep the salmon from the people who refused him.
summary.zh: 郊狼殺雀武士，奪其珠冠；不能解松雞童兒之語，便以松脂封其目。雙親報復，將其嚇落懸崖；郊狼化為木籃，漂至二姊妹之石壩——彼等霸佔全部銀鮭。籃被拾入屋、又被擲入火，火中竟蹦出一小兒。他漸長，頭戴獸角暗掘壩基；水破壩而出，他對泣於岸邊之二女曰：『守鮭者不當為女子。』化二女為水鷸與小水鳥，引鮭上溯。後所戀之回聲少女拒婚，郊狼遂在西米爾卡米恩、奧卡諾根、壺口、哥倫比亞諸河皆築瀑布，以阻鮭上溯，懲罰拒婚之民。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Salmon-liberation cycle, Sanpoil version. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: In the beginning Coyote had great power. He said to himself, 'Why remain in seclusion when I have so much power?' He became restless and wanted to travel, and journeyed down the Columbia River, where he met Sparrow (Chis-ka-ka-nar), a warrior dressed in his beautiful beaded war head-dress, of which he was very proud. As soon as Coyote saw him, he thought, 'I will kill him and take his head-dress.' So he killed Sparrow, took his quiver of arrows and his beaded head-dress, put them on, and felt very brave and proud, resolving to travel close to the river that he might see his reflection.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 101 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: As he came around a bend of the river, he saw blue smoke rising from a tent and called, hoping to find a beautiful maiden to admire him; to his disappointment he saw only twelve children, the Willow-Grouse family, who spoke their own language and could not make him understand that their parents were gathering berries. Coyote became angry, thinking they were calling him names; he gathered pitch and put a piece on the eyes of the children, so that when their parents returned they were all blind. The mother determined to have revenge: she and her husband hid behind bushes by the high cliff and scared Coyote as he came along the edge, singing his war-chant; the roar so startled him that he gave a jump and fell over the cliff. Quickly he turned himself into a basket, which floated lightly on the water below and drifted down with the current.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 101-102 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: At that time two sisters lived by the river, near a solid rock dam which they guarded with jealous care: no one was allowed to come near, and silver-salmon were kept within the dam as their food. Coyote knew of these salmon, and made up his mind to release them. The younger sister (Steneechken) found the basket-dish floating on the water and took it to her tent, though the elder (Wiswiskin) warned, 'Throw it into the river. It may bring us misfortune.' Every day they found the dish empty after their meals, until the elder sister insisted it be thrown into the fire; it made a loud report, and a little boy came out of the fire. They made a bow and arrows for him; each morning after the sisters had left, the boy worked at the dam with a hard rock instrument he had made, and after a month they found him in the form of a man, digging at the hole he had made in the dam, a piece of horn on his head. They tried to crush him, but just then the water broke through and separated him from them. He called to the girls weeping on the bank, 'Women were never intended to guard salmon.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 102 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He started up the stream, and the salmon followed him; he turned one sister into a water-snipe and the other into a kildee — they always live near the water and eat fish. Wherever Coyote met people, he made a salmon jump out of the water into his arms, cooked it, and asked the people to eat. At one place he met a number of beautiful girls picking berries, and fell in love with one who had a fine voice and was in the habit of using it to hear her words repeated by the echo. When Coyote asked her to be his wife, she refused him with scorn; he became angry and started back down the river, taking the salmon with him. He stopped at the Forks of the Similkameen and formed falls to keep the salmon from going up; then he made falls in the Okanagon, Kettle, and Columbia Rivers, because in all these places the maidens refused him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 102-103 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tick and the Deer: Coyote Kills the Many-Armed Wizard
title.zh: 壁蝨與鹿：郊狼誅多臂巫師

region.en: Snowbound hills above the Sanpoil River (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦河上雪嶺（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 2. The Tick and the Deer'

summary.en: Snowbound and starving, Coyote wishes for bones with sinew, then deer-ham, then a bag of fat — each thumping down at his door, brought by a misshapen wizard with many arms who lives over the hill. Coyote follows him, gets a tent nearby by offering to carry water, then kills the old man and flattens him in the rocks — and all the bones jump up and run away, the old man revived, resuscitating the deer-bones and hanging onto the tail of the last deer as it runs. Coyote turns him into a wood-tick, which in spring lives on deer.
summary.zh: 大雪封山，郊狼飢不能寐，許願得骨與筋、鹿腿肉、肥油——皆有人擲至帳前。追蹤至山頂，見形貌怪異、身生多臂之老巫。郊狼佯為挑水傭，得居其側；三日後暗殺老者，壓扁於石堆，棄屍蒿草間。返帳之際，見群骨躍起四竄——老者復活，並救活鹿骨，攀住最後一鹿之尾不放。郊狼化其為木蝨，令其春季寄生於鹿身。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote lived in a tent alone. There was no prospect of food: everything was covered with snow. He stirred up his fire and lay down near it; he wanted to sleep, but was too hungry. He wished for some bones with sinew; just then he heard a noise, went to the door and looked out, and found a bag of bones in front of the tent. He took them in and made some soup, which lasted for several days. Then he was hungry again. He made another wish — deer-ham with chunks of meat — and heard another thump; another bag of bones. He wished for a bag of fat, and it came also. He puzzled over it, and thought that some one must bring this food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 103 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Near him lived a queer old wizard — misformed, with many arms on his body. He knew of Coyote's wishes, and carried the food to him. Coyote decided to watch and see who came; the next time he wished, he stood close by the door and saw the wizard disappearing from sight, and followed him to the top of the hill, where he saw a tent with a platform for drying meat around it. Coyote offered to carry water for the old man if he might be allowed to live there; he was not allowed to live with him, but was given a tent close by. After three days he thought that if he should kill the old man, all the provisions would be his; therefore next morning he followed him to a pile of rocks, pounded him flat, and threw the body into the sagebrush.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 103 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He went back to the tent and was astonished to see all the bones jump up and run away. The old man had revived, and had resuscitated the deer-bones; as the last deer ran away, the old man caught its tail and hung on. Coyote turned him into a wood-tick, and said that in the spring of the year it would live on deer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 103 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Rolling Stone: Coyote Trapped in the Badger-Hole

region.en: Green meadows of the Sanpoil country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦故地青草地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 3. The Rolling Stone'

summary.en: Cricket rattles his wings at a charging buffalo-bull, which bolts blindly over a cliff; the crickets feast on its horn while Coyote arrives wailing that the buffalo was his half-brother, carries them off by his will-power to a green meadow, and compels them to stay there. An old, old woman flatters Coyote into letting her cook the meat, and runs off with it while he naps with both eyes closed; he changes her into a rolling stone — which takes revenge by pursuing him and penning him in a badger-hole. Trapped, Coyote wishes up a crowd of Indians, twelve dogs, twelve tents and a dozen canoes crossing a wide river; the noise draws the rolling stone away — she becomes the grandmother of Cricket and Grasshopper — and Coyote staggers out of the hole.
summary.zh: 蟋蟀振翼，野牛受驚，狂奔墮崖而死。二蟲食其角時，郊狼啼哭而至，謂野牛乃其異父兄弟；以意志攜二蟲至青草之地，令其留居。一老嫗諂媚求為其烹肉，趁其閉目而竊肉而逃；郊狼化之為滾石。滾石復仇，追逐郊狼，終將其封於獾穴之中。郊狼許願召來人群、犬十二、帳十二、舟一打，正渡大河；滾石聞聲而往——竟為蟋蟀與蚱蜢之祖母——郊狼蹣跚出穴。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Cricket and Grasshopper were half-brothers. Cricket went to hunt, and found a spot where the grass was nice and green, through which ran a trail cut deeply by the tracks of heavy animals; Cricket fell into one of these. After a while he heard the tramp of a buffalo-bull; just as the bull was about to step on him, he rattled his wings, which frightened the bull so that it ran down the road and jumped blindly over the cliff, and was killed. Cricket ran after him, descended, and began to feast on his horn. Grasshopper, seeing the fresh buffalo-tracks, thought his brother must be dead and cried aloud; Cricket called him to come down and eat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 103-104 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: As they were enjoying their feast, they heard a whining cry: it was Coyote, mourning for the buffalo — 'Oh, my brother is dead!' he wailed. He told them the buffalo was his half-brother, and begged to be allowed to carry them away; through his magic power he obtained their consent and carried them on his back to the green meadow. The two were suspicious and flew back, but Coyote compelled them to go back, and by his will-power caused them to wish to stay in the meadow. Then he returned to the dead buffalo, cut up the meat, and built a fire to cook some of it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 104 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: While he was busy, an old, old woman came along and told him that he was too great a chief to prepare his own food; she flattered him and persuaded him to allow her to work for him. He lay down with one eye open, but when all was ready he closed both eyes — and when he opened them again, he saw the old woman running off with the meat. He changed her into a rolling stone. Then she took revenge by pursuing him; he ran and ran, tired, and ran into a badger-hole, and the stone rolled onto the mouth of the hole and penned him in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 104 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote thought of his magical power. He wished for five things — a crowd of Indians, about twelve dogs, twelve tents, and a dozen canoes, to be crossing a wide river in the canoes. The noise of the moving people was audible at the place where the bowlder was. Coyote wished the rock to become a woman again, and she began to move; then she arose and went off to see what caused the noise. She was the grandmother of Cricket and Grasshopper. Coyote came out of the hole and staggered away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 104 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: How the Cold Lost its Power

region.en: Ice-lodge in the far north (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 極北冰屋（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 4. How the Cold lost its Power'

summary.en: Northern-Lights has five sons — Cold, Colder, Coldest, Extreme-Cold, and Most-Extreme-Cold — living in an ice-lodge where no heat can be endured. Extreme-Cold, restless, travels south at any season and kills every human being he meets, until the great chief calls a council to regulate the seasons and the shaman South-Wind is chosen to attack him. Meeting Extreme-Cold face to face and withstanding his power for the first time, South-Wind claims kinship — 'Northern-Lights is my sister' — and is admitted to the ice-lodge for the night; the family plans to freeze him while he sleeps, but he gathers pitch-wood and sets it on fire, thawing everything around, and the Cold family perishes in the flames. The shaman broke the power of the cold, and thus the seasons were regulated.
summary.zh: 北極光有五子：寒、更寒、最寒、極寒、絕寒，皆居冰屋，不能耐熱。極寒性動，南遊無時，所遇之人皆死於其手。大神召議，欲定四時，乃選大力巫師南風往討。南風面迎極寒而不損，自稱『北極光乃吾妹』，遂得入冰屋過夜；寒族欲於其睡時凍斃之。南風取松脂薪縱火，四圍盡融，寒族皆焚死。巫師既破寒力，四時乃定。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Season-regulation myth. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Northern-Lights had five sons — Cold, Colder, Coldest, Extreme-Cold, and Most-Extreme-Cold. The youngest son acted as scout; he seared the leaves and grass, and returned to report that he had gone as far as he dared; then the eldest son would finish the work. The other sons stayed in the north with their parents. They lived in an ice-lodge, and could not endure heat of any kind; they were jealous of Extreme-Cold and guarded him well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 104 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: By and by Extreme-Cold became restless and travelled southward. His mother, Northern-Lights, warned him not to speak to any human being; he would kill every one he met. The Indians were much troubled by him, as he came at any season, whenever he wished; therefore the great chief called a council to try and regulate the season. The people could not devise any way of reaching the lodge of Cold; finally South-Wind (Cha-helt), a shaman of great power, was selected to attack him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 105 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He set out, and saw Extreme-Cold approaching; everything perished before him. When he met South-Wind, he tried to exercise his power, but it did not avail him: nobody had ever been able to withstand him. South-Wind held out his hand and addressed Cold as his nephew, saying that he lived in the south and that Northern-Lights was his sister, and asked the way to his sister's house; Cold consented to take him there. When they reached the ice-lodge, Cold was full of steam. South-Wind claimed to be the brother of Northern-Lights, but she said she did not remember him, and her husband declared that they had no relatives. They let him stay all night, and planned to freeze him while he slept; then the Cold family went to sleep. South-Wind gathered pitch-wood and set it on fire; it thawed everything around it, and the Cold family perished in the flames. The shaman broke the power of the cold, and thus the seasons were regulated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 105 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Chipmunk and Meadow-Lark

region.en: Woods of the Sanpoil country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦故地林間（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 5. Chipmunk and Meadow-Lark'

summary.en: An old woman warns her children, Chipmunk and Meadow-Lark, not to go too far into the woods because a hairy monster might kill them; they disobey, and the monster Pcua'nitim shoots Chipmunk, scratching his back as he tries to seize him. Hidden first in a basket, then a bag, the trembling boy is betrayed by his sister Meadow-Lark — bribed with a string of beads she still wears — who sings from the tent-pole, 'Look in the clam-shell under the blanket in the bosom of grandmother!' The monster finds the shell, then marvels at the old woman's fair skin; told she dropped hot pitch on it, he asks to be treated the same way, and she holds him down with two forked sticks and pours the pitch over him until he dies.
summary.zh: 老嫗誡其子女花栗鼠與草地鷚勿深入林中，恐遭毛怪毒手。二童不聽；毛怪 Pcua'nitim 射傷花栗鼠，抓破其背。老嫗先藏之於籃，再藏之於袋，而其姊草地鷚受珠串之賄（今鷚頸珠即其遺），立於帳柱歌曰：『祖母懷中毯下蚌殼裡！』怪遂搜得。怪見老嫗膚白，問其故；嫗答以滾松脂澆身所致。怪求同法；老嫗以二叉棍按住毛怪，滾脂澆之，怪遂斃。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: An old woman (Sti'mtima) had warned her children, Chipmunk and Meadow-Lark, not to go too far into the woods, because a hairy monster might kill them. One day the children disobeyed. The monster shot Chipmunk, and, when trying to seize him, scratched his back. The boy made his escape and hid in his grandmother's tent; she put him first into a basket, then into a bag, but he would not sit still. Soon the monster Pcua'nitim arrived, and searched for Chipmunk; the old woman denied having seen him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 105 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy's sister, Meadow-Lark — bribed with a string of beads that may still be seen around her neck — flew to the pole of the tent, and sang, 'Look in the clam-shell under the blanket in the bosom of grandmother!' The monster took out the shell and found Chipmunk. At the same time he saw that the skin of the old woman was very fair, and asked her, 'What did you do to make your skin so white?' She replied that she dropped hot pitch on it. He asked to be treated in the same way; the old woman heated some pitch and held the monster down with two forked sticks, then poured the pitch over him, so that he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 105-106 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Toad (Sme'nap)

region.en: Tent doorway by a pond, Sanpoil country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦故地水塘畔帳前（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 6. The Toad (Sme'nap)'

summary.en: A woman sits in her tent doorway with her long hair hanging over her face, saying the sun hurts her eyes; when a young man inquires, she puts her arms around him and holds him fast, so that he must carry her wherever he goes. At last he builds a fire and stands so near that her back blisters, her arms relax, and he cuts off her hair — and sees she has no eyes, no nose, no mouth, and looks like a skeleton. He throws her into a pond, and there she becomes a toad.
summary.zh: 一婦坐於帳門，長髮覆面，自稱怕日晒眼。一青年問其故，婦即張臂抱之，強其隨行背負。行遠之後，青年燃火近身炙之，婦背起泡，臂乃鬆，青年斷其髮——竟見其無眼無鼻無口，形同骷髏。遂擲之於塘，化為蟾蜍。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: A woman was sitting in the doorway of her tent. Her long hair was hanging down over her face. A young man wished to see her face. When he inquired why she kept her hair down, she said that the sun hurt her eyes. At the same time she put her arms around him, holding him fast. He had to carry her wherever he went. After walking a long distance, he built a fire, and stood so near the fire that her back blistered. Then her arms relaxed, and the youth cut off her hair. He saw that she had no eyes, no nose, no mouth, and looked like a skeleton. He threw her into a pond, and there she became a toad.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 106 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Origin of Death: The Council Voted

region.en: Sanpoil River villages (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦河村落（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 7. The Origin of Death'

summary.en: During the maturity seclusion of his elder daughter, a father discovers his own son in the girl's tent and kills him by driving a sharp deer-antler point into his ear; the body is laid in a canoe covered with shells and beads and deposited in a cave. The daughter asks for her dress and comb and disappears into the same cave; Fox, Hawk and Eagle try to bring her back but catch only her cape, and the father tells no one. Three days later the Vulture loses his daughter, and asks the chief for power to restore her to life; the chief replies, 'You voted at the council that people should not live forever. This decision cannot be changed because the sorrow has come to one of you yourselves.'
summary.zh: 長女行成年隔離之禮時，父發現其子入女帳，以尖鹿角刺其耳而殺之；屍置舟中，覆以貝珠，藏於巖穴。女索衣裙與梳，遂入同一穴中不返；狐、鷹、雕追之，僅得其披肩，父隱而不宣。三日後兀鷲喪女，求酋長還魂之力；酋長答：『汝等曾於議會決議，人不當長生不死。今禍降己身，其決不可改。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: A man had two daughters and one son. During the maturity ceremonies of the elder daughter, she was secluded. The father discovered his son in the tent of the girl, and killed him by driving a sharp point of deer-antler into his ear. On the following morning the boy was found dead. The body was put into a canoe, covered with shells and beads, and was deposited in a cave. At this time the girl asked for her dress and for her comb, and disappeared in the cave where the body of her brother had been put by. The Fox, the Hawk, and the Eagle tried to bring her back, but they succeeded only in taking hold of her cape. The father did not tell what had happened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 106 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Three days after this the Vulture lost his daughter. He asked the chief for power to restore his daughter to life. The chief replied, 'You voted at the council that people should not live forever. This decision cannot be changed because the sorrow has come to one of you yourselves.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 106 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Skunk and Badger

region.en: Sanpoil trails (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦故地小道（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 8. Skunk and Badger'

summary.en: Badger, afraid of Skunk, feigns death and is carried off over Skunk's shoulder; told the only thing Skunk fears is whistling, Badger whistles — Skunk drops him and his pack of valuables in fright, Badger unties his feet and runs home with the pack. Later, while the people are gambling, Skunk appears, overcomes the gamblers with his scent, and runs away with the stakes Badger had been betting.
summary.zh: 獾懼臭鼬，詐死被負於其肩。行進間，臭鼬自言唯懼哨聲；獾即吹哨，臭鼬大驚，連人帶貴重行囊棄地。獾解縛，負囊而逃。後眾人聚賭，臭鼬現身，以體臭熏倒賭徒，捲走獾所押之贓物。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: A Skunk was travelling along. He found Badger, who, being afraid of Skunk, pretended to be dead. Skunk tied his feet and put him on his shoulder. While they were travelling along, Skunk said, 'The only thing I am afraid of is whistling.' Soon Badger whistled, which scared Skunk so much that he dropped him and the pack of valuable goods that he was carrying. Badger untied his feet, took the pack, and ran home. One day when the people were gambling, Skunk appeared. Badger was betting the goods which he had taken away from Skunk. All of a sudden Skunk overcame the gamblers by his scent, and ran away with the stakes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 106-107 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Five Wolves

region.en: Cliff ledge on the Okanagon River near Oroville (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根河奧羅維爾附近崖臺（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 9. The Five Wolves'

summary.en: A boy crossing the river on a buck's back cuts its throat with a flint knife; five wolves come for the meat, and the grandmother wishes herself, her grandson and the meat up onto a ledge of the cliff near Oroville, leaving dressed rotten wood in the boy's shape below. Unable to reach the ledge, the wolves beg for meat; hot stones wrapped in suet are thrown into their mouths, killing all but the youngest, whose scorched mouth-sides leave the dark marks wolves carry today. Later, needing feathers, the boy sets the two eagles quarrelling over which is swifter, gathers their feathers, and joins the people making war on the sky — transformed into a chickadee.
summary.zh: 童子騎雄鹿渡河，以燧石刀割其喉。狼五隻聞腥而來；祖母施法，偕童與肉升至奧羅維爾附近崖臺，並以爛木扮童留於下方。狼不能攀，乞肉；祖母令童以板油裹燒石擲入狼口，逐一斃之，唯幼狼倖免，口角燙痕即今狼之黑斑。後童箭羽用盡，挑撥雙雕相鬥，拾其落羽，遂隨征天之人同行，化身山雀。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: An old woman and her grandson lived near a river. The grandson wished to cross the river, and called the Deer to take him across; finally an old buck allowed him to mount his back and carried him across. While they were in the water, the boy cut the throat of the buck with a flint knife and killed him. The old woman skinned the buck. Five wolves took the scent of the meat, and came intending to steal it. The old woman dressed a piece of rotten wood in skins, and made it look like the boy; then she wished herself, her grandson, and the meat to be carried to a ledge on the face of a cliff — this cliff is pointed out close to the Okanagon River, near Oroville, Washington.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 107 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the wolves arrived, they attacked the tent, but found that what they believed was a boy was only rotten wood. They were unable to reach the ledge; they tried to jump up, but soon wearied, and then begged for some of the meat. The grandmother told the boy to wrap a hot stone in some suet. He threw it down into the mouth of one of the wolves, and thus killed him; thus all were killed except the youngest. When he caught the hot stone, he could not swallow it, and the fat burned the sides of his mouth — therefore wolves have dark marks at the side of the mouth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 107 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The grandmother and the boy continued to live on the ledge. Finally the boy had used up all his arrows and had no feathers to make new ones; in order to obtain feathers, he caused the golden eagle and the eagle Sinaken to quarrel by telling one that the other claimed to be swifter and stronger than he. The two eagles fought, and the boy gathered their feathers. He told his grandmother that he would join the people who were going to make war on the sky, and he was transformed into a chickadee.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 107 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Origin of Fire: The Arrow-Chain to the Sky

region.en: Arrow-chain from earth to the sky valley (symbolic pin at Sanpoil River)
region.zh: 自大地直達天谷之箭鏈（象徵定位於桑普瓦河）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 10. The Origin of Fire'

summary.en: After rains extinguish every fire on earth, the animals hold a council and resolve to make war on the sky to bring fire back. Coyote tries first and fails; Chickadee's arrows reach the sky and build the arrow-chain up which the animals climb — Grizzly-Bear, last and heaviest, breaks the arrows and is left behind. In the sky valley by the lake where the Sky people fish, Coyote is captured scouting; Muskrat digs drain-holes along the shore, Beaver floats into a fish-trap feigning death, and as the people run out to shoot the eagle overhead, Beaver seizes a clam-shell of glowing coals, jumps into the lake and escapes through the drained water. The arrow-chain home is broken; each bird flies a quadr down on its back, Coyote sails down on buffalo-robe wings he cannot afterwards remove and becomes a bat, and Sucker, jumping, is broken to pieces and refitted with pine-needles in his tail — which is why the sucker has so many bones.
summary.zh: 霪雨滅盡世火，群獸聚議，誓征天族以索火種。郊狼先射不中；山雀連珠射天，箭鏈乃成，群獸攀之而上——灰熊居末，體重斷鏈，未能同行。天谷湖畔，天族漁於水；郊狼充斥候而被擒。麝鼠沿岸掘泄水孔；河貍詐死漂入魚籠，被抬入主帳剝皮；眾人出帳射鷹之際，河貍握蚌殼火炭躍入湖中，經泄水遁去。歸途箭鏈已斷，群鳥各負一獸飛還；郊狼縛牛皮為翼躍下，事後脫翼不得，化為蝙蝠；胭脂魚跳下摔碎，群獸為之拼骨，缺者以松針補其尾——故胭脂魚骨多。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Fire-theft + arrow-chain ascent combination. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once upon a time it rained until all the fires on earth were extinguished. The animals held a council and decided to make war against the sky in order to bring back the fire. In spring the people began, and tried to shoot their arrows up to the sky. Coyote tried first, but did not succeed. Finally the Chickadee succeeded in reaching the sky; he continued to shoot, making a chain of arrows, by means of which the animals climbed up. The last to climb was the Grizzly-Bear, who, on account of his weight, broke off the arrows, and could not join the other animals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 107 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the animals reached the sky, they found themselves in a valley near a lake, where the people of the sky were fishing. Coyote wished to act as scout, but was captured. Then the Muskrat dug holes along the shore of the lake, and Beaver and Eagle set out to obtain the fire. Beaver entered one of the fish-traps and pretended to be dead; they carried him to the chief's house, where the people began to skin him. At this time the Eagle alighted on a tree near the tent; when the people saw the Eagle, they ran out, and at once Beaver took a clam-shell full of glowing coals and ran away. He jumped into the lake, and people tried to catch him in nets, but the water was drained through the holes Muskrat had made.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 107-108 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The animals ran back to the arrow-chain, which they found broken. Then each bird took a quadruped on its back, and they flew down with them. Only Coyote and the Sucker were left above. Coyote tied a piece of buffalo robe to each paw and jumped down; he sailed down on the skin, and finally landed on a pine-tree. On the following morning he showed off his wings, but was unable to take them off again, and was transformed into a bat. The Sucker had to jump down, and was broken to pieces; the animals fitted his bones together, and, since some were missing, they put pine-needles into his tail. Therefore the sucker has many bones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 108 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Eagles: Bald-Head Left on the Ledge

region.en: Eagle-nest ledge between Omak Lake and Omak Creek (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奧馬克湖與奧馬克溪之間鷹巢崖（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 11. The Eagles'

summary.en: Bald-Headed Eagle falls in love with the wife of his elder brother Hail-Storm, and lures him to an eagle's nest between Omak Lake and Omak Creek to gather head-dress feathers; lowered by rope to the ledge, he is deserted by his brother. Attacked by the mother-eagle on her return, he catches her wing and ties her; three days later he ties the male too, ties the young eagles to the same rope, and jumps — carried safely down. His friends then kill the treacherous brother.
summary.zh: 禿首鵰戀其兄雹暴之妻，誘兄同往奧馬克湖與奧馬克溪之間採鷹羽製冠；以繩縋至鷹巢之崖，兄竟棄之而去。母鵰歸巢攻之，其人擒翼縛之；三日後公鵰亦被縛。遂縛雛鵰於同繩，躍崖而下，群鵰負之安全著地。歸後，友人誅其不義之兄。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Gould notes it is told as a true story. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Bald-Headed Eagle (Pakamiaken) fell in love with the wife of his elder brother Hail-Storm (Selusken). One day Bald-Head found an eagle's nest between Omak Lake and Omak Creek. He asked his brother to accompany him and to get feathers for a head-dress. The brothers made a rope, and Hail-Storm let down his elder brother to the ledge on which the eagle's nest was located; there his brother deserted him. He found the young eagles in the nest, and a dead ground-hog which the old eagles had left there. When the mother-eagle returned, she attacked the man, who, however, succeeded in catching her wing and tying her. Three days later the male eagle appeared, and he tied him also. Then he tied the young eagles to the same rope, jumped down, and was carried down safely by the eagles. After he had returned, his friends killed the treacherous brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 108 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Poisoned Arrows: Hesken's Revenge
title.zh: 毒箭復仇：海斯肯誅熊記

region.en: Mountain den of the five grizzly sisters, Sanpoil country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦故地五熊姊妹之山穴（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 12. The Poisoned Arrows'

summary.en: The girl who disobeys her grandmother and picks berries up the brook is killed by the she-grizzly Kelauna; her unborn son is laid unharmed on a rock, found and reared as Hesken by the old woman, who keeps revenge before him. Tested at twelve, he paints a grizzly's head on a rock of power; on a high peak he fasts twelve days, wins a guardian-spirit bird and a song, and is told where to find poison; from his grandfather's spirit, the huge supernatural snake whose eyes shoot lightning, he begs the front tooth — 'Touched with that poison, a victim gives one look and dies.' With five poisoned arrows he waits by the dim trail of the five sisters, chants defiance in the war-lodge of Kimhist — 'I will kill and tear to pieces every grizzly bear I meet' — and picks off the sisters one by one as they climb out at sunrise, scattering their feet to the four winds. The last sister flees through the forest, and he lets her go, deciding not to destroy the whole grizzly-bear race; then Kimhist reveals herself as the spirit of his mother, well pleased with his courage.
summary.zh: 女童違祖母之誡，上溪採莓，為母熊格拉烏納所殺；腹中嬰孩被棄石上而無恙，祖母拾回撫養，取名海斯肯，時時以復仇勉之。十二歲受試，繪熊首於神石；登絕頂絕食十二日，得守護靈鳥與神歌，並獲示毒之所在。至巨蟒之穴——其目閃電、舌吐火——三求毒牙，終得門牙：『觸此毒者，一瞥即斃。』製毒箭五支，伏於五熊姊妹晨出之徑；於金姨之戰舍中朗聲應戰：『凡遇灰熊，必誅而碎之，散其屍於大地！』破曉逐一射殺四姊，斷其足擲於四方，使之不得復返噬人。第五妹遁入林中，海斯肯不追，存灰熊一脈。金姨現身，原為其母之靈，嘉其勇毅。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Monster-slaying hero cycle. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: An old woman warned her daughter not to go up a brook when picking service-berries, because Kelauna, a female grizzly bear, lived there and would attack her. Since berries grew thick and large there, the girl disobeyed; while she picked berries, the grizzly killed her. Her unborn child was laid upon a rock and left unharmed. When the young woman did not return, her grandmother searched for her and found the infant boy, took him home and cared for him, and named him Hesken; when he was a year old she told him of his mother's death, and always kept the idea of revenge before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 109 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he was twelve years old, she wanted to test his courage, and sent him at night to a rock of supernatural power, which he was to mark with a painting of his own design; the next day she found he had drawn a grizzly bear's head. A summer and winter passed; then he was sent across two mountain-ranges, across two valleys, and to a high peak, where he built a monument and remained twelve days without eating or sleeping. His guardian-spirit came to him in the form of a bird, and a song was given to him; he became very brave, and was told by a voice where to find poison with which to tip his arrows to revenge his mother's death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 109-110 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: His grandmother sent him to a distant mountain on which dwelt in a cave a huge supernatural snake: 'When you enter the cave, do not be afraid, although his eyes shoot forth lightning and his tongue flame.' The boy went to the cave and saw the great snake, which lay coiled in the centre. The Snake spoke to him, and he answered, 'I am not afraid of you, for you are the spirit of my grandfather, and I have come to you for poison with which to tip my arrows to avenge my mother's death.' The Snake saw that he had courage and knowledge; he took a tooth from his mouth and offered it to him, but the boy refused it, and another tooth also. He put his arms around the Snake's neck and begged for the real poison, the deadliest the Snake had; then the Snake gave him a front tooth, saying, 'Touched with that poison, a victim gives one look and dies.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 110 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hesken made five arrows and covered the flint tips with poison from the snake-tooth. In the spring he climbed a mountain and found a dim trail made by five sisters; he waited under a pine-tree, then met an old woman named Kimhist, who told him of a war-dance at her house and, after refusing at first — there were five sisters there who did not like strangers — let him come along, telling him to stand behind her back. When they stepped into the lodge there was a heavy growl; the eldest sister, Kelauna, began a chant telling of her intention to destroy every human being in the spring: 'I will kill and tear to pieces every human being I meet, and scatter his body over the face of the earth.' Hesken chanted after her, 'I will kill and tear to pieces every grizzly bear I meet, and scatter his body over the face of the earth.' The woman would have attacked him if Kimhist had not been there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 110 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Before daybreak, while the bears slumbered, Hesken stole out and returned to the tree, climbed it and waited. At sunrise the eldest sister came out of the den, depressed and sad, the tears rolling from her eyes; as she climbed the trail and passed under the pine-tree, Hesken whistled, she looked up, and he killed her with one of his poisoned arrows. He came down, cut off her feet, and threw them to the four winds, scattering them so far that they could not return to devour the Indians of that place. The next morning her sister came out and climbed the trail, and he shot her in the same manner; on the third and fourth days he killed two more of the sisters. On the fifth day the last one came out, but she did not climb the trail; she turned and went off through the forest, and Hesken did not go in pursuit — he decided not to destroy the whole grizzly-bear race. As he descended the mountain he met a black bear, who told him she was Kimhist and the spirit of his mother: 'I was allowed to protect you from the grizzly bears. Now that my death has been avenged, I am well pleased with your courage.' Then she went away. Hesken went back to his grandmother and told her all she had wished to know, and she gave a great feast in his honor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 110-111 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Race between Turtle and Frog

region.en: Rolling meadow race-course, Sanpoil country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦故地起伏草坡賽道（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 13. The Race between Turtle and Frog'

summary.en: A race between Turtle and Frog is proposed over uneven ground, and all the people bet that Frog will win; Mud-Turtle asks three days' grace and bets his back against Frog's tail. Given a head start, Turtle keeps disappearing over the low places ahead of Frog, who hurries faster and faster without ever overtaking him, and crosses the line just as the last low ground is passed. Frog has to give up his tail — it took six turtles to beat him — and now pollywogs have to lose their tails before they can become frogs.
summary.zh: 龜蛙相賽於起伏之地，眾皆押蛙勝；泥龜求三日寬限，以背注蛙尾。龜得先發，每於窪地隱沒復現於前；蛙愈追愈急，終不能及，龜已越線。蛙輸其尾——六龜接力方勝一蛙——故今蝌蚪必先失尾方能化蛙。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: At one time there was a race proposed between Turtle and Frog. All the people bet that Frog would win. Mud-Turtle asked for three days to let his friends know about the race; the race-course was very uneven — low and high ground, rolling meadow. Turtle bet his back against Frog's tail. On the third day Turtle was given a head start. Frog stood there taking more bets; finally he started, and ahead in a low place he saw Turtle going out of sight. Each time he looked ahead he saw Turtle going out of sight; he hurried faster and faster, but did not overtake him. Just as he crossed the last low ground he saw Turtle over the line. He had to give up his tail. It took six turtles to beat him, but he lost the race. Now the pollywogs have to lose their tails before they can become frogs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 111 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Origin of the Different Languages: The Dispute over the Ducks

region.en: Wintering grounds of the ducks on the Sanpoil rivers (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦諸河群鴨越冬之地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 14. The Origin of the Different Languages'

summary.en: Two hunters who have each taken one duck quarrel over whether the whistling-noise the rising ducks make comes from bill or wings, and neither will yield; the chief, whose dead ducks cannot answer, calls a council. The people go down to the river to hear for themselves, and split over the answer — bill or wings — quarrelling violently and separating in an ugly mood. The hatred grows all winter until in spring part of the Indians move south for new homes: the first division of the people into tribes. New objects bring new words, each split brings a new chief and different words and meanings, and thus the tribes slowly scattered, and dialects and even new languages were formed.
summary.zh: 二獵人各得一鴨，為群鴨起飛時之哨聲究竟出自喙或翼而爭執不下。酋長所獲二鴨已死無從對證，遂召集議。眾親往河邊聽之，仍各執一詞，忿然分開。積怨一冬，翌春部分族人南遷覓新居——是為部落之分。新物生新詞，每分一支，即立一酋，言語漸異。諸族由此四散，方言之別乃至新語之立，皆由此起。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Language-separation ethnogony. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: In a certain place in the winter months, the ducks (lulluUo) collected in great numbers; when any one approached them, they would rise and fly away, making a whistling-noise. One morning two hunters went down to a river to kill some ducks; they had each obtained one, when a dispute arose over the question whether the whistling-noise was made with the bill or with the wings when they rose to fly. Neither could convince the other, and the words became bitter; finally they agreed to take it to the chief and let him settle the dispute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 111 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chief heard the story and looked at the ducks; both of them were dead and could not make any noise. Therefore he called a council to listen to the dispute. The people came from all around to deliberate; they spoke one language and had only one chief. The ducks were brought in, and the chief explained the question. The people said, 'We do not wish to be unjust, we will go to the river and hear for ourselves; these ducks can do us no good.' So they went down to the river and frightened the ducks, which flew over their heads. Part of the Indians said the noise was made with the bills; part said it was made with the wings. They could not agree; therefore the ducks were made to fly once more, and the people began to quarrel violently, and separated in an ugly mood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 111-112 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: All during the winter the feeling grew, until in spring the mutual hatred drove part of the Indians south to hunt for new homes. This was the first division of the people into tribes. They selected a chief from their own division, and called themselves by another name. Finding new objects, and having to give such objects names, brought new words into their former language; and thus after many years the language was changed. Each split in the tribe made a new division and brought a new chief; each migration brought different words and meanings. Thus the tribes slowly scattered; and thus the dialects, and even new languages, were formed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 112 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Weeping Woman

region.en: Headwaters of a Sanpoil stream (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦河源頭（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 15. The Weeping Woman'

summary.en: Chatalem lures hunters to their death with her beautiful, sad wailing, always keeping out of sight; one brave hunter follows the stream to its source, camps and sweats there, and when she rises and floats away like a cloud as he approaches, he turns the other way. Later she comes to him unseen while he has killed a deer; in mid-winter he wakes to find her cooking for him — carrying a child with its head down — and she promises to meet him at the forest's edge if he returns alone. His wife insists on accompanying him the next fall, hears the wailing, asks what it is, and he will not tell her; then a high wind and a terrible storm kill her, and the angry hunter returns to his own people and does not go back to the weeping woman.
summary.zh: 恰塔勒姆以哀婉哭聲引獵人送命，始終隱形於視線之外。一勇獵人循溪至源，結廬汗浴；其近前時，婦如雲飄去，他掉頭他往。其後獵鹿之時，婦聲不見形；隆冬一覺醒來，見婦為其炊飯——背上倒懸一孩——並許諾：若獨自歸來，願於林口相候。翌年其妻執意同行，聞哭聲而問，夫不答；旋即狂風暴雨大作，妻為所斃。獵人憤而歸族，不再往見哭泣之婦。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Chatalem lured away hunters by her beautiful, sad wailing. She always kept at a distance from them, so that they could not see her; they followed her until they perished. One brave hunter followed the stream to its source; then he camped and built a sweat-house, and every morning at dawn he heated rocks and took a bath. One morning, when he came back to his tent, he saw a beautiful woman sitting in the doorway. He fell in love with her, and made up his mind to ask her to remain; however, as he approached, she rose and floated away like a cloud, wailing. He was strongly tempted to follow her, but he turned and went the other way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 112 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Later on, she came to him when he had killed a deer; he heard her voice, but did not see her. He thought of her often; he also thought of his wife and children whom he had left at home, and tried to forget her. One day in mid-winter he slept soundly, and when he awoke she was cooking for him; then for the first time he saw her back: she carried a child with its head down. She told him she had come to keep him company, and when he left for home she told him to come back alone, and promised to meet him at the entrance of the forest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 112 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the fall of the year he prepared to go hunting, and his wife wished to accompany him; at first he refused her request, but when she insisted he told her she might go as far as the forest. The next year she desired to accompany him again; as before, he refused, but she insisted. She went as far as the forest, but then she would not return; she followed him and heard a wailing-sound. She asked him what it was, but he would not tell her. Then came a high wind and a terrible storm, and the man's mortal wife was killed. This made the hunter angry, and he returned at once to his own people, and did not go back to the weeping woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 112 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Timtimenee, or the Island of Death

region.en: Island in the River of Death (symbolic pin on the Sanpoil Columbia)
region.zh: 死亡之河中島（象徵定位於桑普瓦哥倫比亞河段）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 16. Timtimenee; or, The Island of Death'

summary.en: A handsome warrior and great hunter takes a plain second wife and brings her most of his meat; the first wife and children starve, the boy sent to the father's tent is rebuffed, and the new wife laughs. The mother whittles three sharp bones from a deer's antler, kills her two children as they sleep, and drives the last into her own breast. Grieved, the father takes his bow and arrows and leaves the camp, crossing the plain to a river with a large island where he sees canoes and camps but no sign of life; a woman comes out of an open tent, paddles across, and he recognizes his first wife, who lands him and takes him into the large tent — inside only skeletons, his children's among them, and then his wife a skeleton too, and himself without flesh. He had crossed the River of Death.
summary.zh: 俊勇獵人另娶陋女，以其居別帳，肉食多歸之。前妻與子女飢寒交迫；其子往父帳求食，遭拒，新婦笑之。母聞子言，削鹿角為三枚銳骨，夜殺二子，最後一枚刺入自己胸膛。父悲痛，携弓箭離營，過平原至一河，河中大島上有舟有帳而無人跡。一婦自開敞之帳出，划舟渡來——乃其前妻。登島入大帳，帳內唯骸骨；子女之骨俱在，妻亦白骨，自顧亦無肉身——原來他已渡過死亡之河。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Contains family-violence narrative as recorded; presented as collected. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was once a camp by a river. Among the people there was a handsome man, who was a brave warrior and a great hunter; he had two children. His wife was beautiful, and he loved her dearly. One day he met a very plain maiden; she attracted him. He took her for his wife, and put her in another tent, and took most of his meat to her. Then the first wife and his children grew hungry; the younger child cried, and the mother sent her son to his father for meat. The boy went to the tent and stood in the doorway; when his father asked him what he wanted, he said that they were hungry. He was sent back without any food, and the new wife laughed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 112 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy returned and told his mother that he had been rebuffed and scolded, and that his father's new wife had laughed at him. His mother listened to his words, took a deer's antler, and whittled three sharp bones out of it. With two of these she killed her children while they were asleep; the last one she drove into her own breast. In the morning the grandmother of the children came with food and found them dead. She raised a wail, and the people came to see what had happened; then the father was grieved. He took his bow and arrows and left the camp.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 112 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He crossed the plain, and came to a river in which was a large island. He saw canoes and camps on it, but he did not see any signs of life. He became sleepy. One tent on the island was open; a woman came out, boarded a canoe, and paddled across. He recognized his first wife, who took him across. They landed, and she pulled the canoe up on shore; she took him into the large tent. Inside there were only skeletons. He saw his children's skeletons. Then he saw that his wife too was a skeleton. He looked at himself, and he saw that he had no flesh. He had crossed the River of Death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 113 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Starvation: The Elk that Appeared at Sunrise

region.en: Snowbound camp of the Sanpoil winter (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦故地雪冬之營（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 17. Starvation'

summary.en: Deep snow, no game; hearing his wife tell the children 'Your father may bring us some nice meat to-day,' a hunter is too downcast to enter his own tent. In a dream a voice tells him, 'Don't leave this place! Awake, and look towards the rising sun!' — and at sunrise an elk appears, which he shoots; whenever he needs meat, an elk appears, and in this way they live through the winter.
summary.zh: 大雪封山，獵無所獲。獵人歸而未入帳，忽聞妻對子女言：『你父親今天或許會帶好肉回來。』他羞慚欲絕。夜夢中有聲音說：『勿離此地！醒來朝東方日出處看！』日出之時，麋鹿自現，一箭而獲；此後每有所需，鹿必自現。一家遂安然度過嚴冬。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: One winter there was a very heavy snow, and the people were starving. A man lived alone with his wife and children; on account of the snow he was unable to kill any game. One night when he returned, he heard his wife saying to the children, 'Your father may bring us some nice meat to-day.' He felt very much downcast when he heard this, and went back without entering the tent. He lay down to sleep, and in his dream he heard a voice saying, 'Don't leave this place! Awake, and look towards the rising sun!' When he awoke and the sun rose, an elk appeared, which he shot. Whenever he needed meat, an elk would appear. In this way they lived through the winter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 113 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote, Wren, and Grouse

region.en: Ridge and cliff above Pend d'Oreille country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 彭德奧雷伊故地山嶺與斷崖（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Michel Revais; collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Pend d'Oreille Tales, 1. Coyote, Wren, and Grouse'

summary.en: Coyote mocks Wren's tiny bow — 'You can't shoot far with those' — and Wren promises to shoot him on the distant ridge, where the arrow strikes his heart; Fox pulls out the arrow and jumps over him, and Coyote comes to life claiming a long nap. Later Coyote gambles everything away from Wren, sings 'I won from the Kalispel,' cooks the ten grouse children in a hole in their own lodge, and is ambushed by the revenged parents and Wren on a ridge by a steep cliff: one grouse flies at his head, another between his legs, and he falls over the cliff while they pluck him of his winnings as he falls, restoring everything to Wren, who restores the children to life.
summary.zh: 郊狼譏鷦鷯弓小射不遠；鷦鷯言能於遠嶺射中其心。郊狼果於嶺上中箭斃命；狐拔箭躍其身，郊狼復活，自稱久眠。其後郊狼賭盡鷦鷯弓箭衣物，唱『我勝了卡利斯佩爾人』；又於松雞家中掘坑，以燒石烹其十個孩子。松雞夫婦與鷦鷯合謀復仇：於崖嶺上，一雞撲其面，一雞穿其襠，郊狼墜崖；眾雞趁其墜落拔光其贏來之物，歸還鷦鷯；鷦鷯則令松雞孩子復生。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Pend d'Oreille narrative told by Michel Revais and recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once Coyote met Wren (tsEska'n), and laughed at his small bow and arrows. He said, 'You can't shoot far with those.' Wren answered, 'Yes, I can shoot far. If you go to that distant ridge, I will shoot you while you are there.' Coyote laughed, and said, 'That ridge is so far away that we can hardly see it.' Soon afterwards Coyote was walking along this ridge, and Fox was following him; he had forgotten about his talk with Wren. Presently he heard something coming, and Wren's arrow struck him in the heart; he gave two jumps and fell down dead. Fox pulled out the arrow, and jumped over Coyote, who came to life, and said, 'I must have slept a long time.' Fox said, 'You were not sleeping, you were dead. Wren's arrow struck your heart. Why do you fool with Wren? You know he can shoot better than any one.' Coyote took the arrow from Fox, and said, 'I shall get even with him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 114 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some time after this, Coyote met Wren, and proposed to gamble with him: 'I have an arrow which looks like yours. Now you have a chance to win it back.' They played a game of throwing arrows; Coyote beat Wren every time, won all his arrows, then his bow, and later all his beautiful clothes. Wren was left practically naked. Coyote went off singing, 'Alpano'n e Kalispe'' ('I won from the Kalispel'), and Wren followed him at some distance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 114 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote passed by the lodge of Willow-Grouse, who had ten young children, their parents being off in the hills. He mocked their parents' names, went into the lodge, dug a small hole near the fire, and said to the children, 'Carry those red bearberries into the hole, and watch me cook them for you.' They did so, and crowded around the edge to watch him; he pushed them into the hole and threw earth and hot ashes on top of them, then went on. Their parents came home and, finding their children dead, they cried. Wren came along and told them, 'I have a grudge against Coyote, too. I want my things which he won from me.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 114-115 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: If you can get them back for me, I will restore your children to life.' Coyote was then passing over a high ridge, close to a steep cliff. Grouse made a detour, and hid ahead of him on the upper side; when Coyote was opposite them, one flew out suddenly at his head — he bent back over the cliff to avoid it — then the other flew between his legs, and he lost his balance and fell over the cliff. Grouse hastened and plucked him as he was falling: they plucked away his bow and arrows and quiver and clothes, and gave them back to Wren, who restored the children to life.
